what: One set of creative controls for copy, video and pictures. The core dials apply to every medium; a few belong to one medium (film and picture grammar) and say so. Each dial is a 0 to 4 scale with a named anchor at every level; the same dial means the same thing in every medium and every chain. A reader measures the level an asset is at; a chain sets the level it should be at.
source: the owner 2026-10-23: standardize the creative controls across copy, video and images; turn them up and down; absurd, maxed out, hyper-specific by default. Researched: psychology (valence, arousal, emotion, incongruity, benign violation, vividness, persuasion knowledge, authenticity, attention) and practitioner vocabulary (creativity templates, visual rhetoric, comedy and rhetoric craft).
rule: A machine reads these dials from here and never restates them. The delivery dials (humor kind, delivery style, register, pacing) say how a piece sounds; these say how far it goes.
default_rule: Unless a preset or the brief says otherwise: intensity, absurdity, specificity, dramatisation and stopping power at the top, swap depth at replacement, ad-likeness at native. Maxed and hyper-specific is the house stance; the guards keep it on the claim. The floor (never sterile) holds under every preset.

guards.name: Relevance
guards.what: Every absurd or swapped element is about the problem, the result or the product. Unexpected and irrelevant is the one quadrant that hurts the message (Heckler & Childers).

guards.name: Legibility
guards.what: The problem and what is ours read inside a second, however loud the rest is (Pieters, Warlop & Wedel).

guards.name: Benign
guards.what: Every violation carries its safety: distance, a character, obvious exaggeration (McGraw & Warren).

guards.name: Claim-safe
guards.what: Exaggerate the premise and the emotion, never the medical or physical outcome.

guards.name: Receipt
guards.what: Every hyper-specific detail comes from the avatar's own words or the brand's own files; none is invented.

guards.name: Never sterile
guards.what: Every ad clears the floor on intensity, absurdity, humor, dramatisation and stopping power, at every awareness level. A proof or offer ad gets its proof inside an absurd, dramatised picture, never a plain product shot.

guards.name: Reads cold
guards.what: The words on the ad make sense to a stranger on one read, before any joke lands (the owner, 2026-10-23, on a picture otherwise called great: "the text on that image doesn't make sense"). A borrowed sentence shape is kept only when our words still say something literally true and clear inside it; never fill the swipe's sentence with our nouns like a word game. If the line needs the swipe to be understood, rewrite it.

guards.name: One idea
guards.what: The words and the picture say the same thing. A stranger who reads the line and then looks at the picture understands why that picture is there (the owner, 2026-10-23: "tie the image and copy together to make sure they actually make sense"). A line about something the picture does not show fails, however good it is alone.

guards.name: Parody, not copy
guards.what: A real brand mark, outfit or famous face the swipe carries is turned into an absurd parody of itself, never kept as the real thing and never blanked. We are making people laugh, never passing anything off (the owner, 2026-10-23).

dials.name: Intensity
dials.what: How hard the piece hits the body: heart rate, not mood. Separate from whether the feeling is good or bad.
dials.framework: The activation axis of Russell's circumplex of affect; Berger & Milkman found high-activation emotions get shared, whatever their valence.

scale.name: flat
scale.what: Calm, sleepy, nothing moves.

scale.name: low
scale.what: Mild, conversational, a shrug.

scale.name: engaged
scale.what: Alert; something is at stake.

scale.name: high
scale.what: Heart-rate up: anger, disgust, a burst of laughter, a wince.

scale.name: peak
scale.what: Shock, scream, can't-look-away; the strongest version of the feeling the ad carries.

dials.copy: Short sentences, hard verbs, stakes named, capitals and punctuation used sparingly but at the peak.
dials.video: Cut rate, camera motion, loudness, the performer's energy; the peak lands in the first three seconds.
dials.image: Contrast, saturation, how much of the frame the subject fills, how tight the crop, how much motion is implied.

default.why: Activation is what makes people stop and share; a low-arousal ad is wallpaper.

dials.risk: Peak arousal with no relief reads as distress; 3 against 4 is worth testing.

research.cite: Russell 1980, circumplex model of affect
Berger & Milkman 2012, What makes online content viral?

dials.name: Valence
dials.what: Whether the feeling is unpleasant or pleasant. Set per beat: a direct-response piece usually opens low and closes high.
dials.framework: The valence axis of Russell's circumplex.

scale.name: aversive
scale.what: Repulsive or threatening: the problem at its worst.

scale.name: uneasy
scale.what: Tension, discomfort, a cringe.

scale.name: neutral
scale.what: Informational, no push.

scale.name: pleasant
scale.what: Warm, light, relieved.

scale.name: euphoric
scale.what: Triumph, delight, the payoff.

dials.copy: Loss against gain framing; the words of the problem against the words of the result.
dials.video: Faces, music key and tempo, colour grade, and the arc from the open to the close.
dials.image: The face, colour temperature and light, cramped and dark against open and bright.

default.why: At the open: the problem at its worst stops the right person. The close moves up the scale.

dials.risk: Disgust sticks to whatever it touches: keep the -2 on the problem, never on the product.

research.cite: Russell 1980, circumplex model of affect
Morales & Fitzsimons 2007, product contagion

dials.name: Absurdity
dials.what: How far the piece breaks what should happen. Always tied to the claim: absurd and relevant, never absurd and random.
dials.framework: Schema incongruity (Mandler; Meyers-Levy & Tybout), split by Heckler & Childers into unexpected and relevant: only unexpected-and-relevant helps the message.

scale.name: expected
scale.what: The category's usual picture.

scale.name: twist
scale.what: One unexpected detail inside a real scene.

scale.name: incongruous
scale.what: An odd premise, explained in the same beat.

scale.name: absurd
scale.what: Impossible but read in a second; the impossible thing IS the benefit or the problem.

scale.name: surreal
scale.what: Dream logic, rules broken on purpose, still pinned to the claim.

dials.copy: Impossible comparisons, absurd specifics, a non sequitur the payoff line resolves.
dials.video: A scene that breaks physical or social rules (giant objects, the wrong setting, deadpan wrongness) and a clean beat that resolves it.
dials.image: Scale distortion, one impossible object in an otherwise real photo, a swapped object that should not be there.

default.why: Maxed and hyper-specific is the house stance; the relevance guard keeps it on the claim.

dials.risk: Originality can pull attention to the ad and off the brand; the moderate-incongruity sweet spot failed a pre-registered replication, so test 3 against 4.

research.cite: Heckler & Childers 1992, expectancy and relevancy
Meyers-Levy & Tybout 1989, schema congruity
Pieters, Warlop & Wedel 2002, Breaking through the clutter

dials.name: Humor
dials.what: How much the piece is played for a laugh. The kind of humor is the delivery dial's humor value; this dial is how far it goes.
dials.framework: Benign violation (McGraw & Warren): something is wrong and safe at once. Speck's typology runs from comic wit to full comedy.

scale.name: none
scale.what: Played straight.

scale.name: wry
scale.what: A smile; light wit.

scale.name: playful
scale.what: Clearly a joke, warm.

scale.name: edged
scale.what: A sharp violation made safe by distance, a villain or a target.

scale.name: full comedy
scale.what: A sustained gag; violation and safety both at the top.

dials.copy: Set-up and punch, rule of three, deadpan specifics, self-deprecation.
dials.video: Timing, the performer, the reaction shot, escalation; the strongest medium for it.
dials.image: A visual pun or a one-frame gag; the caption carries the punch.

default.why: The problem is already a violation; humor is what makes it safe to look at.

dials.risk: A violation with nothing benign about it reads as gross or offensive.

research.cite: McGraw & Warren 2010, benign violations
Speck 1991, humorous message taxonomy

dials.name: Specificity
dials.what: How exact the piece is: a named time, place, number, object and body part against a general claim.
dials.framework: The vividness effect (Nisbett & Ross), dual coding (Paivio), imagery processing (MacInnis & Price).

scale.name: abstract
scale.what: A general claim.

scale.name: category
scale.what: A category-level detail.

scale.name: concrete
scale.what: One sensory detail or one named situation.

scale.name: hyper-specific
scale.what: A named place, number, time, object or body part.

scale.name: a movie in one frame
scale.what: Two or more senses, an exact moment and an exact number or object.

dials.copy: Nouns over adjectives, numbers, sensory verbs.
dials.video: Macro on the exact detail, real texture, the proof moment on screen.
dials.image: Every swapped or exaggerated element at a stated size, texture and colour; real detail visible, never stock.

default.why: Specific beats general, and it is what keeps absurd and dramatised pieces believable.

dials.risk: A specific detail that is invented reads false; every one comes from the avatar's own words or the brand's files.

research.cite: Nisbett & Ross 1980, the vividness effect (summary: Smith & Shaffer 2000)
MacInnis & Price 1987, imagery in information processing

dials.name: Dramatisation
dials.what: How far the problem, the reaction or the result is pushed past life size.
dials.framework: Hyperbole and figurative language (Kronrod & Danziger), puffery (Xu & Wyer), and the demonstration tradition: show the effect, bigger.

scale.name: literal
scale.what: States the fact.

scale.name: emphasis
scale.what: A strong word or framing, still plausible.

scale.name: dramatised
scale.what: Acted reaction, pushed before and after, still possible.

scale.name: hyperbole
scale.what: Physically impossible and obviously figurative.

scale.name: heightened reality
scale.what: The effect staged at its extreme and shown, not said.

dials.copy: Hyperbole, extreme comparison, the specific consequence.
dials.video: Staged reaction, speed ramp, dramatic reveal, the exaggerated demo.
dials.image: The problem or product oversized, the extreme before and after, the strongest expression.

default.why: Obviously non-literal exaggeration is the drama; it reads as a picture, not a claim.

dials.risk: Exaggerated outcomes are where ad policy and believability break: push the premise and the emotion, never the medical result.

research.cite: Kronrod & Danziger 2013, figurative language and hedonic consumption
Xu & Wyer 2010, puffery in advertisements

dials.name: Swap depth
dials.what: How deeply our thing is merged into the source picture. Climbs from showing two things side by side to replacing one with the other.
dials.framework: Phillips & McQuarrie's visual rhetoric typology: juxtaposition, fusion and replacement, in rising complexity; Goldenberg's replacement template; Forceville's pictorial metaphor.

scale.name: literal
scale.what: Our thing shown as itself; nothing borrowed.

scale.name: juxtaposed
scale.what: Our thing placed beside the borrowed one, the viewer compares.

scale.name: fused
scale.what: Our thing and the borrowed one merged into one object.

scale.name: replaced
scale.what: The borrowed object is gone; ours stands in its place and the scene still reads.

scale.name: replaced world
scale.what: Several objects swapped by one rule, so the whole scene becomes ours.

dials.copy: Simile at 1, metaphor at 2 and 3, an extended metaphor carried through the whole piece at 4.
dials.video: Match cut at 1, morph at 2, the object swapped in the swipe's own footage at 3, the swipe's world rebuilt in our terms at 4.
dials.image: The picture swap: keep the swipe's pose, light, crowd and frame; swap the meaning-carrying objects by shape and role.

default.why: Replacement keeps the swipe's proven picture and makes it ours in one look.

dials.risk: Replacement is the hardest to read; if the swapped object does not rhyme in shape and role the picture goes random.

research.cite: Phillips & McQuarrie 2004, beyond visual metaphor: a typology of visual rhetoric
Goldenberg, Mazursky & Solomon 1999, the fundamental templates of quality ads
Forceville 1996, Pictorial Metaphor in Advertising
van Enschot et al. 2022, refining replacements
Forceville 2008, pictorial and multimodal metaphor

dials.name: Edge
dials.what: How much the piece breaks a social rule: the thing people don't show or say. The violation half of benign violation.
dials.framework: Benign violation: the violation must be strong enough to register and distant enough to stay safe.

scale.name: polite
scale.what: Nothing anyone would hesitate to post.

scale.name: candid
scale.what: Says the thing people usually leave out.

scale.name: uncomfortable
scale.what: Shows what people hide: the close-up, the confession.

scale.name: gross or taboo
scale.what: Repulsive or forbidden, held at a distance.

scale.name: shocking
scale.what: The line most brands won't cross, made safe by absurdity or a character.

dials.copy: The unsaid thing said plainly; the confession; the name nobody uses in public.
dials.video: The close-up nobody films, the reaction held too long.
dials.image: The problem shown at full size, in full light.

default.why: The problem is the edge; showing it is the whole point.

dials.risk: Ad review rejects some edges outright; above 3 the benign half must be obvious.

research.cite: McGraw & Warren 2010, benign violations
Morales & Fitzsimons 2007, product contagion

dials.name: Realism
dials.what: How real the world of the piece looks, independent of how absurd its event is. A real man in a real bathroom with an impossible thing in it is realism 3, absurdity 4.
dials.framework: Authenticity as cues the viewer reads (Beverland & Farrelly); the video chain's realism index rows.

scale.name: stylised
scale.what: Cartoon, CGI, obviously built.

scale.name: polished
scale.what: Studio, believable but idealised.

scale.name: casual pro
scale.what: Natural light, real location, light edit.

scale.name: lo-fi real
scale.what: Phone-shot, imperfect frame, real skin, unscripted feel.

scale.name: documentary
scale.what: Raw, unvarnished, a real person, place and moment.

dials.copy: Speech rhythm, hesitation, slang from the room; never marketing tone.
dials.video: Handheld, available light, a real room, imperfect delivery; the realism index's production rows.
dials.image: Real skin texture, unretouched, candid frame, phone grain. On a 3D set, realism is the print's job: the print turns the set's grey shapes into real materials, wear and grain.

default.why: Lo-fi real makes the absurd land as something that happened, and keeps it off AI slop.

dials.risk: The UGC-beats-polished evidence is thin; treat it as our own test, not a law.

research.cite: Beverland & Farrelly 2010, the quest for authenticity

dials.name: Ad-likeness
dials.what: How much the piece looks like an ad. 0 is a post a friend could have made; 4 is a commercial.
dials.framework: The persuasion knowledge model (Friestad & Wright): once people see it is an ad, they discount it. Native-ad studies find recognition lowers evaluation.

scale.name: native
scale.what: Indistinguishable from an organic post: no price, no offer, no call to action.

scale.name: native with product
scale.what: Organic form, the product present, not pitched.

scale.name: hybrid
scale.what: Creator-style form with an offer or call to action.

scale.name: ad-coded
scale.what: Product hero, claims, price, call to action.

scale.name: commercial
scale.what: Broadcast polish, logo first.

dials.copy: First person and story first at 0; headline claims and offer at 3.
dials.video: Selfie framing, platform captions, no title card at 0; logo, music bed and polish at 4.
dials.image: A screenshot, a note, a meme, a real post at 0; a button graphic, price badge and packshot at 3.

default.why: Upper funnel is not supposed to feel like an ad at all. Bottom funnel sets its own level.

dials.risk: Paid-partnership rules still apply; the dial is about form, never about hiding who pays.

research.cite: Friestad & Wright 1994, persuasion knowledge model
Wojdynski & Evans 2016, Going native

dials.name: Stopping power
dials.what: How hard the first second stops the scroll, and whether the thing that stops it is ours.
dials.framework: Attention research (Nelson-Field; Lumen) and distinctive brand assets (Romaniuk); originality grabs attention but can steal it from the brand (Pieters, Warlop & Wedel).

scale.name: wallpaper
scale.what: Nothing catches the eye.

scale.name: noticeable
scale.what: One salient element: a colour, a face, motion.

scale.name: sometimes stops
scale.what: A clear hook inside the first second.

scale.name: interrupt
scale.what: An unexpected picture or sound in frame one, the problem or product readable early.

scale.name: hard stop
scale.what: An unmissable break in the first second, ours to own, and a reason to keep looking.

dials.copy: The first five words: a pattern break, specific, an open loop.
dials.video: Frame one and the first three seconds: motion, a face, an odd picture, a sound.
dials.image: One dominant focal point, high contrast against the feed, a face or an odd object; words readable in a glance.

default.why: Everything else is wasted if the scroll does not stop.

dials.risk: Score the hook and its link to us separately; a stop on something unrelated is a wasted click.

research.cite: Nelson-Field 2020, The Attention Economy (coverage)
Pieters, Warlop & Wedel 2002, Breaking through the clutter

dials.name: Relevance
dials.what: How tightly the strange part connects back to the problem, the result or the product. The partner every loud dial needs.
dials.framework: Ad creativity is divergence AND relevance together (Smith et al.); only unexpected-and-relevant helps the message (Heckler & Childers).

scale.name: unrelated
scale.what: Curiosity only; the weird part has nothing to do with us.

scale.name: loose
scale.what: A vague association.

scale.name: mapped
scale.what: The strange part stands for one clear feature or problem.

scale.name: mapped with proof
scale.what: It stands for the feature and shows it working.

scale.name: the weird IS the demo
scale.what: The strange part is itself the demonstration of the problem or the result.

dials.copy: The punchline lands on the product's point.
dials.video: The impossible event is the product doing its job.
dials.image: The swapped object is the problem or the product, not decoration.

default.why: The safety rail that lets everything else run at the top.

dials.risk: At 0 or 1 the ad buys clicks with no intent behind them.

research.cite: Smith, MacKenzie, Yang, Buchholz & Darley 2007, divergence and relevance in ad creativity
Heckler & Childers 1992, expectancy and relevancy

dials.name: Rhyme
dials.what: How closely our swapped object matches what it replaced in shape, pose, colour, size and light. The reason a swap reads in one look.
dials.framework: Visual rhyme, one of the four picture figures McQuarrie & Mick tested; its film cousin is the graphic match.

scale.name: no rhyme
scale.what: Our object looks nothing like what it replaced.

scale.name: loose
scale.what: Similar role, different shape.

scale.name: shape
scale.what: Same outline or silhouette.

scale.name: shape and place
scale.what: Same shape, same position and scale in the frame.

scale.name: perfect rhyme
scale.what: Same shape, place, scale, light and colour: the eye slides from theirs to ours.

dials.copy: Same rhythm and length as the line it replaces.
dials.video: A graphic match: the cut lands on the same shape.
dials.image: The ball becomes the product in the ball's place, angle and light; the product stays its true size and the rhyme in frame size comes from where it sits in the 3D set (nearer the camera reads bigger), never from scaling the product.

default.why: A swap that rhymes reads as the swipe first and ours a second later.

dials.risk: Forcing a rhyme can deform the product; the product stays true to itself and true to size. In the set, move the camera or the product's place to match the old object's frame size; never resize the product's own build.

research.cite: McQuarrie & Mick 1999, visual rhetoric in advertising (rhyme, antithesis, metaphor, pun)
Forceville 2008, pictorial and multimodal metaphor

dials.name: Coherence
dials.what: How tightly the words and the picture make one idea. Measured on the finished ad; a chain aims for the top.
dials.framework: Image-text congruence and anchorage (Barthes); in ad research, picture and headline that share one meaning are processed faster and remembered better than ones that pull apart.

scale.name: unrelated
scale.what: The words and the picture are about different things.

scale.name: loose
scale.what: The same topic, no shared point.

scale.name: captioned
scale.what: The words describe the picture, the joke lives in one of them only.

scale.name: linked
scale.what: The words name what the picture shows and add to it.

scale.name: one idea
scale.what: Neither works without the other: the line pays off exactly what the eye just saw.

dials.copy: The headline names the picture's swapped object or moment.
dials.video: The line on screen or spoken pays off the shot it sits on.
dials.image: The caption explains why that picture is there.

default.why: A great picture under a line that makes no sense is a wasted picture.

dials.risk: Spelling out the picture word for word kills the joke; anchorage stays low while coherence stays high.

research.cite: Barthes 1964, Rhetoric of the Image (anchorage)

dials.name: Anchorage
dials.what: How much the words tell the viewer what the picture means. Low makes the viewer solve it; high spells it out.
dials.framework: Barthes's anchorage: text fixes the meaning of an image. With the swap's structure it sets the inference load (Phillips & McQuarrie).

scale.name: no words
scale.what: The picture alone carries it.

scale.name: a hint
scale.what: A few words point the way.

scale.name: a caption
scale.what: The words name the subject, not the link.

scale.name: the link named
scale.what: The words say what the swap means.

scale.name: explained
scale.what: The words explain the whole picture.

dials.copy: How much the headline gives away.
dials.video: Whether the voice or captions explain the picture.
dials.image: The caption's job: solve it or leave it.

default.why: A picture the viewer solves is remembered; one hint keeps it readable.

dials.risk: At 0 a hard swap can go unread; at 4 the picture stops working.

research.cite: Barthes 1964, Rhetoric of the Image (anchorage)
Phillips & McQuarrie 2004, beyond visual metaphor: a typology of visual rhetoric

dials.name: Borrowedness
dials.what: How much the piece is a known picture, format or moment the viewer already recognises.
dials.framework: Intertextuality (allusion, pastiche, parody, remix); figure effects fade when viewers lack the cultural knowledge (McQuarrie & Mick).

scale.name: original
scale.what: Nothing borrowed.

scale.name: allusion
scale.what: A nod to something known.

scale.name: homage
scale.what: The look of a known thing.

scale.name: parody
scale.what: A known thing reworked for a laugh or a point.

scale.name: remix
scale.what: A known picture or format, kept, with our objects swapped in.

dials.copy: A known line or meme phrasing reused.
dials.video: A known format, scene or trend reused.
dials.image: A known photo or meme template kept, objects swapped.

default.why: A picture they already know stops them; the swap makes it ours.

dials.risk: If the viewer does not know the source the joke falls flat; pick sources from the avatar's own feed.

research.cite: McQuarrie & Mick 1999, visual rhetoric in advertising (rhyme, antithesis, metaphor, pun)
Culture jamming / détournement

dials.name: Shot scale
dials.what: How close the camera is to the subject.
dials.framework: Film shot scale; Kress & van Leeuwen read closeness as social distance.

scale.name: extreme wide
scale.what: The subject small in a big world.

scale.name: wide
scale.what: The whole body and place.

scale.name: medium
scale.what: Waist up.

scale.name: close-up
scale.what: A face or a hand fills the frame.

scale.name: extreme close-up
scale.what: Skin, pores, one bump.

dials.copy: Not used.
dials.video: The size of the subject in each shot.
dials.image: How much of the frame the subject fills.

default.why: Close is intimate and shows the problem; wide is for scale gags.

dials.risk: Too close loses the scene a swap depends on.

research.cite: Film grammar: shot scale, average shot length, camera movement
Kress & van Leeuwen, Reading Images (demand and offer, social distance)

dials.name: Eye contact
dials.what: Whether the person looks at the viewer.
dials.framework: Kress & van Leeuwen: a look at the lens is a demand, no look is an offer to be watched.

scale.name: unaware
scale.what: No idea a camera is there.

scale.name: glance
scale.what: A passing look.

scale.name: candid
scale.what: Profile, caught in the moment.

scale.name: to lens
scale.what: Looks at the viewer.

scale.name: direct address
scale.what: Talks or gestures straight at the viewer.

dials.copy: Second person against third person.
dials.video: Talking to camera against being watched.
dials.image: The eyes on the lens or on the problem.

default.why: Candid reads native; to-lens reads as a pitch.

dials.risk: Direct address raises ad-likeness.

research.cite: Kress & van Leeuwen, Reading Images (demand and offer, social distance)

dials.name: Density
dials.what: How much is in the frame.
dials.framework: Minimalism against maximalism in visual art and internet aesthetics.

scale.name: minimal
scale.what: One subject on nothing.

scale.name: sparse
scale.what: A subject and a hint of place.

scale.name: balanced
scale.what: A scene.

scale.name: dense
scale.what: Many things competing.

scale.name: maximal
scale.what: Packed edge to edge.

dials.copy: Word count on the ad.
dials.video: How busy each frame is.
dials.image: How many things the eye has to sort. In a 3D set every level has a real surface under the subject; density counts the props on it, from one (0) to edge to edge (4).

default.why: One thing to look at makes the swap land.

dials.risk: Dense frames hide the problem. Themed props add to density: dress surfaces before adding objects.

research.cite: Internet aesthetics vocabulary (cursed, liminal, deep-fried, maximalism)

dials.name: Scale distortion
dials.what: How far an object's size breaks reality.
dials.framework: Scale distortion (Magritte, Oldenburg); Goldenberg's dimensionality alteration.

scale.name: true size
scale.what: Everything life size.

scale.name: slightly off
scale.what: A little big or small.

scale.name: noticeable
scale.what: Clearly too big or small.

scale.name: monumental
scale.what: A building-sized object.

scale.name: impossible
scale.what: Planet-sized, or a city in a palm.

dials.copy: Size words that break reality.
dials.video: The giant object in the scene.
dials.image: The giant bump, the tiny man, the monumental prop. Built in the 3D set: the distorted thing is modelled at its distorted size and the print gives it real contact and shadow; never asked of the picture model in words, which cannot hold a size.

default.why: Scale is the cheapest way to absurd that still reads.

dials.risk: The product at the wrong size against itself breaks the one-product-one-size rule. Distort a prop, a problem or the world around the product; the product's own build stays at its true size unless the whole joke is one giant product, shown once.

research.cite: Goldenberg, Mazursky & Solomon 1999, the fundamental templates of quality ads
Internet aesthetics vocabulary (cursed, liminal, deep-fried, maximalism)

dials.name: Uncanny
dials.what: How strange or wrong the picture feels, short of absurd: something is off.
dials.framework: Internet aesthetics: liminal, uncanny, cursed images.

scale.name: wholesome
scale.what: Nothing off.

scale.name: slightly off
scale.what: A small wrongness.

scale.name: liminal
scale.what: An empty, in-between feeling.

scale.name: uncanny
scale.what: Almost real, unsettling.

scale.name: cursed
scale.what: Disturbing and compelling.

dials.copy: Not used.
dials.video: The off feeling in the room or the face.
dials.image: The cursed-image look: flash, odd angle, wrong detail.

default.why: A little off stops the scroll; cursed can read as AI slop.

dials.risk: Above 2 it starts to look generated.

research.cite: Internet aesthetics vocabulary (cursed, liminal, deep-fried, maximalism)

dials.name: Degradation
dials.what: How worn the image itself looks: grain, compression, filters.
dials.framework: Internet aesthetics: deep-fried and low-quality memes; the lo-fi look.

scale.name: clean
scale.what: Sharp, clean file.

dials.name: Parody marks
dials.what: What happens to the real logos, outfits and famous faces a swipe carries.
dials.framework: Parody and pastiche (intertextuality); the knock-off as a joke the viewer is in on.

scale.name: real
scale.what: The real mark or the real person, untouched. Never.

scale.name: blanked
scale.what: Removed: plain gear, no face. Safe and dead.

scale.name: slight twist

scale.name: rebuilt from the problem

dials.copy: A parody brand name in the words when the picture carries one.
dials.video: Parody marks on wardrobe and props; lookalikes, never the real person.
dials.image: Every logo, crest, outfit and famous face in the swipe becomes its parody.

default.why: the owner, 2026-10-23: the parody is part of what makes it funny and culturally relevant.

dials.name: Culture casting
dials.what: How much the piece casts the people and moments the avatar already knows: celebrities, known influencers, memes and moments from the avatar's own feed, as lookalikes and references.
dials.framework: Intertextuality and borrowed interest: a figure or moment the viewer recognises earns attention and shares; the joke lands when it comes from the viewer's own culture (McQuarrie & Mick; the parody lookalike matrix).

scale.name: anonymous
scale.what: Generic people, no cultural reference.

scale.name: nod in the words
scale.what: A known line, meme or moment named in the words only.

scale.name: nod in the picture
scale.what: A known look, setting or moment in the background or styling.

scale.name: lookalike lead
scale.what: A celebrity or known-influencer lookalike from the avatar's world carries the piece: a recognisable nod with a slightly different face, never the real person.

scale.name: built on the moment
scale.what: The whole piece is built around a known figure or cultural moment the avatar's world is talking about right now.

dials.copy: The words reference a known person, meme or moment from the avatar's feed.
dials.video: A lookalike of a known figure from the avatar's world plays the lead; the scene borrows a moment the viewer knows.
dials.image: A lookalike of a known figure from the avatar's world in the picture; the swipe's own famous people kept as lookalikes.

default.why: the owner, 2026-10-25: "we should always try to use celebrity / known influencer lookalikes and other cultural references in what we make. it helps drive engagement while being funny and aware of the audience"; "should be in the chain".

dials.risk: A lookalike too close to the real person reads as the real person (the owner, same day, on a famous bald lookalike: the face slightly different); one from outside the avatar's feed falls flat. Keep the face slightly different; pick figures from the avatar's researched worlds.

dials.name: Dressing
dials.what: How far one concept, taken from the avatar's culture map and crossed with the moment (a season or holiday), dresses the swipe's frame: its surfaces, props, palette and the words printed on props. The layout, camera and reading path never move; only what things are made of changes.
dials.framework: Set dressing and production design in film; moment (topical) marketing; the culture-concept method the promotion emails already prove.

scale.name: as swiped
scale.what: The swipe's own surfaces, props and colours, untouched.

scale.name: moment prop
scale.what: One prop that marks the swipe's moment becomes the same prop for ours, same size and place.

scale.name: moment palette
scale.what: The moment's palette on the surfaces, plus the moment prop.

scale.name: concept world
scale.what: Every surface and prop is made from one concept's world, at true size, the moment's name on one real prop.

scale.name: the world built
scale.what: The whole frame is the concept's world, down to the textures, with the layout still the swipe's.

dials.copy: The headline is the concept talking, with one spice device; never the sale's dates as a calendar.
dials.video: The scene's set, props and wardrobe dressed for the concept; the format's shots unchanged.
dials.image: Built in the 3D set before the print: concept surfaces and props at true size, the moment's palette on them, the moment's name printed on a real prop (a flag, a sign, a tag).

default.why: the owner, 2026-10-28: image ads, "especially for promotion", are "supposed to actually stand out on feed and be themed". A native post stays at 1: never restyled into a cleaner set.

dials.risk: Dressing that moves the layout breaks the swipe; dressing on a native post makes it read as an ad. Clutter kills the one idea: dress surfaces before adding props.

emotions.video: The blade on raw skin, the sharp inhale.

technique_rule: Techniques are switches: a piece uses one or it does not. They are how a dial gets turned up; name the one used.

techniques.name: Juxtaposition
techniques.what: Two things side by side so the viewer makes the link.

techniques.name: Fusion
techniques.what: Two things merged into one object.

techniques.name: Replacement
techniques.what: One object stands in the place of another the scene expects; the context says what is missing.

techniques.name: Extreme situation
techniques.what: The product or problem in an absurd, unrealistic situation that makes the attribute obvious.

techniques.name: Extreme consequence
techniques.what: Show what happens after, pushed to the extreme: the consequence of having it or not having it.

techniques.name: Competition
techniques.what: The product pitted against something from another world to show its strength.

techniques.name: Interactive experiment
techniques.what: The viewer is made to do or test something in the ad.

techniques.name: Dimensionality alteration
techniques.what: Time, size or number changed: years later, a thousand of them, a giant one.

techniques.name: Scale distortion
techniques.what: One object at an impossible size against real things.

techniques.name: Visual pun
techniques.what: A picture that reads two ways at once.

techniques.name: Heightening
techniques.what: Find the one unusual thing and make it bigger each beat.
techniques.source: Improv craft (the game of the scene)

techniques.name: Rule of three
techniques.what: Two set the pattern, the third breaks it.

techniques.name: Misdirection
techniques.what: Lead to one reading, land on another.

techniques.name: Deadpan
techniques.what: The absurd played completely straight.

techniques.name: Understatement
techniques.what: The extreme described as minor.

techniques.name: Hyperbole
techniques.what: The minor described as extreme, obviously not literal.

techniques.name: Personification
techniques.what: The problem or product given a person's face or will.

techniques.name: Native format
techniques.what: Built in a form the feed already carries: a screenshot, a note, a meme, a post.

techniques.name: Extreme analogy
techniques.what: The swapped symbol pushed to an extreme instead of only transplanted.

techniques.name: Integrated metaphor
techniques.what: Our object posed so it looks like the thing it stands for, without being changed.

techniques.name: Visual rhyme
techniques.what: Two different things pictured with the same form.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.what: Two opposites side by side.

techniques.name: Pun
techniques.what: One word or picture, two meanings.

techniques.name: Détournement
techniques.what: A known image or ad reused with its meaning changed.

techniques.name: Defamiliarisation
techniques.what: The familiar made strange so it is seen fresh.

techniques.name: Omission and suggestion
techniques.what: Leave the key thing out; the viewer fills it in.

techniques.name: Without words
techniques.what: The picture carries everything; no copy.

techniques.name: Repetition and accumulation
techniques.what: Many of the same thing; one is different.

techniques.name: Callback
techniques.what: A later beat returns to an earlier one.

techniques.name: Non sequitur
techniques.what: A beat that does not follow, resolved by the payoff.

techniques.name: Anti-joke
techniques.what: The set-up promises a punchline and delivers a plain fact.

techniques.name: Status reversal
techniques.what: The high-status one ends up lowest, or the other way round.

techniques.name: Tag / button
techniques.what: One more small laugh after the main one.

techniques.name: Match cut
techniques.what: A cut that matches shape, colour or movement across shots.

techniques.name: Jump cut
techniques.what: A cut inside one shot that skips time.

techniques.name: Smash cut
techniques.what: An abrupt cut from one extreme to another.

techniques.name: Point of view
techniques.what: The camera is the viewer's own eyes.

techniques.name: Found footage
techniques.what: Looks like footage nobody meant as an ad.

techniques.name: Text overlay
techniques.what: Words on the picture carry the hook.

techniques.name: Early proposition
techniques.what: The point lands in the first three seconds.

techniques.name: Seeds of curiosity
techniques.what: A line that opens a question the next line answers.

techniques.name: Slippery slide
techniques.what: Each line exists to get the next one read.

techniques.name: Reason why
techniques.what: Every claim given its reason.

techniques.name: In-world signage
techniques.what: Words printed on a real prop in the scene (a flag, a shop sign, a tag, a receipt) carry the moment's name; built into the 3D set and printed with it, so the words sit on the prop's surface with its light. Only the moment's own name, big and plain; the headline is still set on top.
techniques.source: Film and theatre: diegetic text; the 2026-10-28 Black Friday flag

techniques.name: Moment dressing
techniques.what: The props and colours that mark the swipe's own moment become the same props and colours for ours: same object, same size, same place (a national flag on a dowel becomes the sale's flag on the same dowel).

techniques.name: True-scale set
techniques.what: The swipe's scene is built in 3D at real sizes with its camera and light, then printed into a photo: sizes, depth, contact and light come from the set, never from words. What makes scale distortion and rhyme possible without the product looking pasted on.

interactions.rule: High arousal drives sharing whatever the valence; valence picks the emotion, intensity drives the spread.
Absurdity at 3 or 4 only works with the relevance and legibility guards met.
Edge above 2 needs humor or absurdity to make it benign; without it the same picture reads as gross.
Dramatisation at 3 or 4 is paired with specificity and realism at 3 or more, or it reads as puffery.
Low ad-likeness delays the 'this is an ad' discount; absurdity and humor may lower it further. A hypothesis for our own tests.
Dressing changes what things are made of, never where they are: a dressed swipe that moved a zone, the camera or the product's place is a different ad. Native posts keep dressing at 1.
interactions.source: Stage 3 injection v13, THE CONCEPT; the owner, 2026-10-25 and 2026-10-28

presets.name: Native, unaware
presets.what: Upper funnel: a post, not an ad; no offer, no call to action.

presets.name: Problem aware
presets.what: The problem shown and named, the cause revealed.

presets.name: Product proof
presets.what: Bottom funnel: proof, the result, the price when called for, carried inside an absurd, dramatised picture. Never a plain packshot.

floor.what: Never sterile (the owner, 2026-10-23: "we don't want any sterile ads at all. This is Q4 money season"). No preset, saved level or brief may set these dials below these levels, at any awareness level, bottom funnel and offers included. Parody marks never below 2: a real mark or face is never kept, and never just blanked.

bar_rule: The bar (the owner, 2026-10-23, on the first run made with these controls: "this is what I'm talking about. These statics are brilliant ... this is actually my style of marketing"). Five moves, written as moves, never as the ads themselves: a chain reads them as the level to reach, then finds its own swipe's version. Copying one is a failure of the same kind as a sterile ad.

bar.name: The borrowed world, rebuilt from the problem
bar.move: A famous meme picture is kept whole (the person, the pose, the sky, the caption block) and its world is rebuilt out of the problem itself: the ground becomes the problem's own texture at monumental scale, and the one big object in the sky becomes a single giant instance of the problem. The words say exactly that, plainly.

bar.name: The avatar's own simile, made literal
bar.move: The problem is drawn exactly the way the avatar describes it in their own words (if they say it feels like a pattern, the problem is laid out in that pattern), on a native phone selfie, captioned with the roast they actually hear. One element is blown up to impossible size so the cause is visible.

bar.name: The blamed thing, by the warehouse
bar.move: The thing the viewer blames for the problem is multiplied into a whole stocked warehouse, pallets and shelves of it; our product is held up in front of it by a real hand. The offer rides inside the joke, never on a plain sale graphic.

bar.name: The ranking, hijacked
bar.move: A familiar ranking format (a tier list) holds every fix the viewer has tried, standing on the problem itself as the background; our product sits alone in the top tier, and the line says the winner was not even one of the usual answers.

bar.name: The explainer that comes off the board
bar.move: A hand-drawn explainer board compares the old way and ours; one drawn element turns real and loops out of the drawing into the room, so the cause is literally coming off the board. The real product sits beside it, true to how it rests.

bar.name: The swipe, dressed as the moment's world
bar.move: A sale swipe is kept exactly (layout, camera, the hero product's place) and every surface and prop is rebuilt at true size from one concept the avatar already loves, crossed with the moment: the moment's palette on the surfaces, the moment's name on a real prop in the scene, the swipe's boxes as the brand's own closed boxes, the real product at its true size. The headline is the concept talking, the offer exactly as ordered.

arc_rule: The awareness level picks the arc (best_for). Every beat of the arc holds one section from the marketing doctrine's list, so the arc IS the section plan. After the last beat, the close follows as the awareness level asks (offer, call-to-action, urgency where it is true). One arc per piece; a borrowed swipe keeps its arc unless the brief says why it changes.

arcs.name: Person in a hole
arcs.how: The most-shared emotional shape in a 1,700-story corpus; the fall makes the rise feel earned.

beats.beat: Falls in: the problem hits, it gets worse
The way out (the product as the rope)

arcs.source: Vonnegut, 'Shapes of Stories' lecture ('man in a hole'); Reagan et al. 2016, EPJ Data Science

arcs.name: Rags to riches
arcs.how: Pure aspiration with no dip; it carries on momentum and a strong before-and-after picture.

beats.beat: Low start, shown in a specific detail
Each step up, each one visible

arcs.source: Reagan et al. 2016 (the six core arcs)

arcs.name: Icarus
arcs.how: Schadenfreude plus the fear of being that person: it sells prevention and is the arc of most public scandals.

beats.beat: The lead ignores the warning sign

arcs.name: Cinderella
arcs.how: The arc with the most reliably positive response in the corpus; the middle loss sets up the end.

arcs.name: Oedipus
arcs.how: Shows the failed solutions, so the real one lands as the only one left.

beats.beat: The false fix that seems to work

arcs.source: Reagan et al. 2016; Schwartz on failed solutions

arcs.name: Story circle
arcs.what: A circle out and back, changed.
arcs.how: Every satisfying story leaves and comes back changed; the circle makes a 30 s ad feel complete.

beats.beat: Return: goes back to where it started

arcs.source: Dan Harmon, the story circle (after Campbell)

arcs.name: Save the cat beats
arcs.what: Three acts with a midpoint and a dark night.
arcs.how: The commercial-film standard; its last frame mirrors its first so the change can be seen.

arcs.name: Hero's journey
arcs.what: Departure, ordeal, return with the gift.
arcs.how: The viewer is the hero; the brand is the mentor, never the hero.

beats.beat: Meeting the mentor (the side character with the fix)

arcs.source: Joseph Campbell (1949); Christopher Vogler, The Writer's Journey; Donald Miller, StoryBrand

arcs.name: Kishotenketsu
arcs.how: Holds attention with surprise instead of conflict; built for the absurd and the surreal.

beats.beat: Ketsu: the twist and the set-up click together

arcs.source: Classical Chinese and Japanese four-part composition

arcs.name: But / therefore
arcs.what: Every beat caused by the last.
arcs.how: Beats joined by 'and then' feel like a list; joined by 'but' and 'therefore' they feel like a story, and nobody scrolls in the middle of one.
arcs.source: Trey Parker & Matt Stone, NYU masterclass (2011)

arcs.name: Cold open
arcs.what: The climax first, then how we got here.
arcs.how: The open question ('how did it get here?') holds the viewer through the set-up they would otherwise skip.
arcs.source: Horace, Ars Poetica (in medias res); TV cold-open practice

arcs.name: Mystery box
arcs.what: A question first, the answer last.
arcs.how: An unanswered question is felt as a gap that has to be closed; the viewer watches to close it.

beats.beat: An image or line that cannot be explained yet
Clues, each one raising the question

arcs.source: J. J. Abrams, 'The mystery box' (TED 2007); Loewenstein 1994

arcs.name: Epiphany bridge
arcs.what: The teller's story leads to the same realisation the viewer needs.
arcs.how: A viewer accepts a belief discovered inside a story far more easily than one they are told.

beats.beat: The epiphany: what I found out
The result, and who I am now

arcs.name: Escalation ladder
arcs.what: One absurd idea, pushed further every beat.
arcs.how: Each step is surprising but follows the rule the viewer learned on step one, so it feels inevitable and funny.

beats.beat: Biggest, past the point of sense

arcs.source: Upright Citizens Brigade, 'the game' (Besser, Roberts & Walsh, UCB Comedy Improvisation Manual)

arcs.name: Micro-drama
arcs.what: Hook, conflict, reversal, cliffhanger, every minute.
arcs.how: The vertical-drama apps hold viewers for hours with a reversal every 60-90 s; the satisfying comeuppance is the reward.

beats.beat: Hook: a betrayal or a shock in the first second
A cliffhanger or a satisfying humiliation of the villain

arcs.name: Two sides
arcs.what: The same event told twice, differently.
arcs.how: The viewer becomes the judge; judging is engagement, and the gap between versions is the joke.

arcs.name: Unreliable narrator
arcs.what: The lead tells it one way, the picture shows another.
arcs.how: The viewer is ahead of the character, which feels clever and holds the viewer to the moment the character catches up.

beats.beat: Everyone but the lead can see it

arcs.source: Wayne Booth, The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961)

arcs.name: Transformation reveal
arcs.how: The held before is the tension; the drop on the beat is the release, and it is the frame people screenshot.

beats.beat: The before, held long enough to feel
The process, sped up or hidden
The drop: the after, on a beat

device_rule: Story devices are switches inside the arc: name each one used. A device that is set up must be paid off.

story_devices.name: Open loop
story_devices.what: Start a story or question and leave it unfinished; an interrupted task stays in the mind until it is closed.
story_devices.how: Open two loops in the first 5 s and close the second one last.

story_devices.name: Curiosity gap
story_devices.what: Show the viewer there is something they do not know yet, and that it is about them.
story_devices.how: Name the gap precisely ('the one thing every pro in the trade knows that you don't') so it feels small enough to close by watching.

story_devices.name: Question hook
story_devices.what: Open on a question the viewer answers in their head.
story_devices.how: Ask the question the viewer is embarrassed to ask out loud.

story_devices.name: Pattern interrupt
story_devices.what: Break what the feed has trained the eye to expect: wrong scale, wrong place, wrong sound.
story_devices.source: Neuro-linguistic practice; attention research on novelty
story_devices.how: Combine it with the curiosity gap so the interrupt asks a question.

story_devices.name: Ticking clock
story_devices.what: A visible time limit: the date, the meeting, the mirror before leaving the house.
story_devices.how: Put the clock on screen; cut faster as it runs down.

story_devices.name: Raise the stakes
story_devices.what: Every beat costs the lead more: from comfort, to a date, to a job, to their name in public.
story_devices.how: Make the last stake social and public: who sees it.

story_devices.name: Reversal
story_devices.what: The situation turns into its opposite: the winner is losing, the bully is humiliated.
story_devices.how: Put the reversal on a cut and a sound hit.

story_devices.name: Recognition
story_devices.what: The character realises the truth, usually about themselves.
story_devices.how: Show it on the face, held; it is the frame the viewer identifies with.

story_devices.name: Set-up and payoff
story_devices.what: Something shown early that matters at the end.
story_devices.how: Plant the product or the clue in the first 5 s so the ending feels earned, not sold.

story_devices.name: False victory
story_devices.what: The lead thinks it is fixed; it is not.
story_devices.how: Make the failed fix the competitor's category (the usual tool everyone already tried) and let it fail on screen.

story_devices.name: All is lost
story_devices.what: The lowest point just before the turn.
story_devices.how: Strip the sound or the colour at the low point; the product arrives after it, never before.

story_devices.name: Twist
story_devices.what: A late fact that changes the meaning of everything before it.
story_devices.how: The twist must be fair: one clue earlier that the viewer only notices on a second watch (rewatches count).

story_devices.name: Cliffhanger
story_devices.what: End a section on an unresolved peak.
story_devices.how: In a series, end each part on one; in one ad, end each verse on one.

story_devices.name: Want versus need
story_devices.what: The lead wants one thing (respect, the date); the lead needs another (to stop hiding).
story_devices.how: The ad delivers the want by solving the need.

story_devices.name: The flaw
story_devices.what: One specific, human flaw the viewer shares: vanity, denial, pride.
story_devices.how: Make the flaw funny, never contemptible; the viewer must like the lead.

story_devices.name: Save the cat moment
story_devices.what: A small kind or relatable act early, so the viewer is on their side.
story_devices.how: Even the villain-of-the-story gets one if it is the lead.

story_devices.name: The villain
story_devices.what: The problem as a character: the tool that fails, the bad advice, the doubter.
story_devices.how: Never a real person or a real competitor by name; a category or a personified thing.

story_devices.name: The mentor
story_devices.what: The side character who hands over the fix: the pro, the elder, the friend.
story_devices.how: The mentor is who the brand plays; the viewer stays the hero.

story_devices.name: The witness
story_devices.what: Someone else reacts to the problem or the change, so the viewer sees it through their eyes.
story_devices.how: The witness shows what the hero cannot: the friend's wince, the date's double take.

story_devices.name: The confession
story_devices.what: The lead admits something to the camera that they hide from everyone else.
story_devices.how: Start on the confession; it is a pattern interrupt and an open loop at once.

story_devices.name: Emotional whiplash
story_devices.what: Swing from one emotion to its opposite in one cut: laughing to wincing, shame to pride.
story_devices.how: One swing per 10 s keeps arousal up; arousal drives sharing.

story_devices.name: Peak and end
story_devices.what: People remember the most intense moment and the last moment, not the average.
story_devices.how: Design one peak and make the last 2 s the best feeling in the ad.

story_devices.name: The specific detail
story_devices.what: One detail so exact it can only be true: the receipt, the timestamp, the brand of the cheap thing that failed.
story_devices.how: One per beat; specific beats general every time.

story_devices.name: Identity mirror
story_devices.what: The viewer sees themselves in the character's exact situation.
story_devices.how: Use the avatar's own words from research, word for word.

story_devices.name: Callback ending
story_devices.what: The last frame or line returns to the first, changed.
story_devices.how: Same framing, same line, opposite meaning.

story_devices.name: The tag
story_devices.what: One more joke after the story is over.
story_devices.how: Put the product or the offer in the tag so the laugh carries it.

story_devices.name: The receipt
story_devices.what: Hard proof on screen at the moment of doubt: the close-up, the real result, the real date.
story_devices.source: Schwartz on verification; DR proof practice
story_devices.how: Show it when the viewer's doubt peaks, not at the end.

trigger_rule: Persuasion triggers are why a story turns into a click. Each row says how far to push and where the line is; the line is a guard, never a dial. A trigger used without its truth (a fake deadline, a fake crowd) is refused.

persuasion_triggers.name: Narrative transportation
persuasion_triggers.what: A viewer absorbed in a story argues back less and takes on its beliefs.
persuasion_triggers.line: The claim inside the story must still be true.
persuasion_triggers.how: Deliver the claim inside the story, never as a break from it.

persuasion_triggers.name: Social proof
persuasion_triggers.what: People do what people like them are doing.
persuasion_triggers.line: Real numbers and real customers only.
persuasion_triggers.how: Show a crowd of people like the viewer, in the viewer's world, doing it.

persuasion_triggers.name: Authority
persuasion_triggers.what: We follow people who look like they know.
persuasion_triggers.line: Never a fake credential; an actor is a character, never claimed as a real expert.
persuasion_triggers.how: The pro, the doctor, the elder who has seen it all: a role the viewer already trusts.

persuasion_triggers.name: Scarcity
persuasion_triggers.what: Things feel more valuable when they might run out.
persuasion_triggers.line: Never a fake countdown or fake stock.
persuasion_triggers.how: Tie it to a real moment: the season, the event, the real stock.

persuasion_triggers.name: Loss aversion
persuasion_triggers.what: A loss hurts about twice as much as the same gain feels good.
persuasion_triggers.line: No fear about a health problem the viewer does not have.
persuasion_triggers.how: Frame what the viewer keeps losing: the photos deleted, the plans skipped.

persuasion_triggers.name: Commitment and consistency
persuasion_triggers.what: After a small yes, a bigger yes is easier.
persuasion_triggers.line: Never trick anyone into a commitment.
persuasion_triggers.how: Ask a question the viewer answers yes to in their head, then another, then the click.

persuasion_triggers.name: Unity
persuasion_triggers.what: We say yes to people who are 'us'.
persuasion_triggers.line: Never fake membership in a real community or culture.
persuasion_triggers.how: Speak as one of their own: their slang, their world, their references.

persuasion_triggers.name: The reason why
persuasion_triggers.what: A request with a reason gets more yeses, even a thin reason.
persuasion_triggers.how: Always give the mechanism: why it works, in one line.

persuasion_triggers.name: Contrast and anchoring
persuasion_triggers.what: A thing is judged against what is shown next to it.
persuasion_triggers.line: The anchor must be a real alternative at a real price.
persuasion_triggers.how: Show the expensive, painful alternative first, then ours.

persuasion_triggers.name: Future pacing
persuasion_triggers.what: Let the viewer picture themselves after, in a specific moment.
persuasion_triggers.line: Never promise a result the product does not give.
persuasion_triggers.how: One exact future scene: the photo posted, the compliment received.

persuasion_triggers.name: Identity shift
persuasion_triggers.what: People act to match who they think they are.
persuasion_triggers.line: Never shame who the viewer is now.
persuasion_triggers.how: Sell who the viewer becomes, not the tool: 'the one who never hides anymore'.

persuasion_triggers.name: Reciprocity
persuasion_triggers.what: We return favours, even small ones.
persuasion_triggers.line: A gift with no strings, really.
persuasion_triggers.how: Give something real first: the tip, the free quiz result.

persuasion_triggers.name: The common enemy
persuasion_triggers.what: A shared enemy bonds the viewer to whoever names it.
persuasion_triggers.line: Never a real competitor by name or a group of people.
persuasion_triggers.how: The enemy is the problem or the old way, never a person.

edge_line.what: How far to go: to the edge, never over. Push everything on the left; nothing on the right, ever.
push: Exaggeration and absurdity everyone can see is a joke
Real public stories, told as what was publicly reported, allegations labelled
Real fears and real embarrassment, shown honestly
Lookalike archetypes and cultural nods, never the real person
Uncomfortable truths about the problem, the category and the old way
never: A claim the product cannot back
A fake testimonial, review, crowd, expert or result presented as real
A fake deadline, fake stock or fake price
A real person named, impersonated or defamed
Mocking a health condition, disability, race, religion or any protected trait
A real tragedy used for laughs
Shame aimed at the viewer instead of at the problem
edge_line.source: Workspace rulings (claim-safe, benign, parody-not-copy guards); FTC endorsement guides; Meta advertising standards

story_interactions.rule: Unaware viewers get curiosity arcs (cold open, mystery box, kishotenketsu, escalation); problem-aware get the fall (man in a hole, Icarus); solution-aware get the failed fixes (Oedipus, epiphany bridge); product- and most-aware get the reveal (transformation, rags to riches).
The more the piece feels like a story, the less the viewer argues with the claim; break the story to sell and the resistance comes back.
An absurd piece still needs one turn; absurdity with no change is a meme, not an ad.
Two arcs in 30 s read as noise; nest a device inside the arc instead.
The last 2 s decide how the whole ad is remembered; never end on the offer alone, end on the feeling with the offer on it.
